pr_title: portabled: add parameters for layered images support
pr_body:
Add an --extension parameter to portablectl, and new DBUS methods
to attach/detach/reattach/inspect.
Allows to append separate images on top of the root directory (os-release
will be searched in there) and mount the images using an overlay-like
setup (unit files will be searched in there) using the new ExtensionImages
service option.

Fixes #14697
pr_comments:
RFC because as mentioned in https://github.com/systemd/systemd/issues/14697#issuecomment-670639429 : 

> here's my current thinking on this - now that MountImages has been merged as a primitive, duct-taping it in portabled is easy enough, and in fact I've got it working with a small diff that adds --root and --app-mount-point parameters to portablectl and a new dbus attach method. It works, all is well.
> 
> But - it seems to be it doesn't fit nicely with how images are handled for portabled and nspawn. It doesn't work with discovery and metadata extracting, as only the application image is linked in the portables/machines directory. It feels a bit shoe-horned in.
> 
> So what about the following instead. Establish a parent directory where all application images get mounted in, inside the guest namespace - eg: /run/systemd/app/ (or any other path that fits). And then -
> 
> for single-filesystem images:
> 
> extend /etc/portables and friends to support a drop-in hierarchy structure
> if foo.raw and foo.raw.d/bar.raw are present, foo.raw is RootImage and bar.raw is MountImages on /run/systemd/app/bar/
> same for directory-based images
> os-release is searched in foo.raw, units/nspawn commands are searched for in bar.raw
> for GPT images:
> 
> add a new partition GUID for app partitions, where the label is the name of the application and thus the mount point /run/systemd/app/
> os-release is searched for in the root partition, units/nspawn commands are searched for in the app partition
> What's nice about this scheme is that the next logical step could then be multiple application volumes/services/runners with a single root image, all sharing the same namespaces. Something like pods for podman/k8s.
> 
> Thoughts?

But before I set out to do the extra work, I'd like some feedback. The current implementation as is in this PR works for my purpose, but I think there's scope to do something better.

> F: mksquashfs not found

Don't the bionic images have squashfs-tools installed? How can it be added?

Hmm, can you elaborate the use case here? i.e. you want to run portable services that are actually the combination of multiple images, i.e. one main image plus a number of additional images mounted in? With an example, how is that supposed to look like in the end?

This PR seems to suggest the main image downloaded is actually going to be one that is mounted into a subdir, instead of the root? What#s the logic behind that? Or am I misunderstanding something?

> Hmm, can you elaborate the use case here? i.e. you want to run portable services that are actually the combination of multiple images, i.e. one main image plus a number of additional images mounted in? With an example, how is that supposed to look like in the end?
> 
> This PR seems to suggest the main image downloaded is actually going to be one that is mounted into a subdir, instead of the root? What#s the logic behind that? Or am I misunderstanding something?

@poettering  essentially yes - it was a while ago now, but if you remember we talked about this at FOSDEM. The linked RFE has all details, but the summary is that my current use case is similar to what Flatpak/Snaps and others do - a common runtime as the root and each application has its own image on top of that. The use case is the same as other projects implementing the same pattern - I own the runtime env and need to service it faster than application owners can for security updates and so on.

There are different ways to implement this, and there are 3 alternatives I am proposing, in increasing order of complexity and features provided.

The simplest way is what this PR implements - the new --root-image param is where os-release is searched in and it's used with RootImage, and the existing image param is where the units are searched in and it's mounted on the --mount-point path. This is the code as submitted here, it's the bare minimum required to make this work with no modelling.

This is how it looks like on the cmdline:

```portablectl attach --root-image some-distro.raw --mount-point /run/app/foo foo.raw```

Which gets foo.service from foo.raw and uses RootImage=some-distro.raw and MountImages=foo.raw:/run/app/foo in the portable.conf generated drop-in.

Then aside from the current implementation, the question I'm asking is whether a stronger modelling is desirable, with a fixed mount point instead of a custom parameterized one, and structuring it in /etc/portables as subdirectories. So the second way, more complex but with a better defined model as a feature, could look like this:

```portablectl attach --app foo.raw some-distro.raw```

It would result in this under /etc/portables/ :

```
uuid-some-distro.raw
uuid-some-distro.raw.d/foo.raw
```

Then as the last pattern with even more features (which I've already been asked for informally) it would be possible to do a podman style "pod", where multiple services run not only with the same runtime/root but also sharing namespaces. It feels like the natural next step for the current set of features.

It would look something like the following:

```portablectl attach --app foo.raw --app bar.raw some-distro.raw```

It would result in this under /etc/portables/ :

```
uuid-some-distro.raw
uuid-some-distro.raw.d/foo.raw
uuid-some-distro.raw.d/bar.raw
```

Then too.service from foo.raw will get RootImage=some-distro.raw and MountImages=foo.raw:/run/systems/portables/foo and same for bar.raw with an extended JoinNamespaces directive.


At the moment, the current implementation as you see here fits my requirements. But working on this I got thinking about the above, and I'd really like to hear feedback about all of this, and what you think makes the most sense here. Thanks!

hmm, i am not a big fan of overlayfs, but it might be OK as long as things are "mostly ready-only". hence: wouldn't it make sense for RootImage=/path/to/foo.raw to automatically set up overlayfs /path/to/foo.*.overlay.raw onto it?

Or, maybe better: instead of using overlayfs actually "leaf merge" all file systems `/path/to/foo.*.extra.raw` on top of `/path/to/foo.raw`. By "leaf merge" I mean that we'd first mount foo.raw (let's call this one "base"), and then look into foo.*.extra.raw (let's call these ones "extensions") and iterate through all files/dirs in the extensions that are "leaf inodes" in the base. by leaf inodes i mean files or empty dirs, i.e. all inodes that have no further children. 

This would mean, let's say the base contains a typical os tree:

```
/etc/passwd
/etc/group
/usr/bin/ls
/usr/lib64/libc.so.6
/usr/lib/os-release
/opt
/var
…
```

and now extension `#1` contains:

```
/opt/myapp/bin/foobar
```

and extension `#2` contains:

```
/usr/lib/os-release
```

These three files would then be assembled so that /opt/ from extension #1 would over-mount /opt/ from the base, since /opt prefix of /opt/myapp/bin/foobar that is a leaf. And /usr/lib/os-release would over-mount /usr/lib/os-release from base, since that is the leaf that is the prefix of the same path, if you follow what i mean.

This model has some shortcomings though: everything you add needs to exist as mount point in the base already.

or hmm, maybe a combination of both models could work, i.e the "leaf merge model" and the "overlayfs model". mount the extensions as simple bind mounts if the deepest existing prefix in the base image is a leaf inode, as already suggested. But if the deepest existing prefix in the base image does not exist, then do an overlayfs mount on the deepest common prefix of both images. And then, declare that any such mounts are strictly read-only, i.e. extensions will only ready-only extend the base, and writable changes may only be made to the base where not obstructed by an extension.

I kinda like that model I must say. It would not require any new directives, but be entirely implicit: you could extend any image like this with more stuff, and the code for it should be reasonably simple still.

Not a huge fan of overlayfs either, but most importantly there's some conflict with the combination of LSMs I have to use, IPE and SELinux, which means I've got a hard requirement of things working without overlayfs unfortunately. I'll see what I can come up with that uses the same model you are proposing, but without overlay. Should be possible in principle.

what kind of conflict is that? isn't that something one can fix?

i think overlayfs is actually fine, if used entirely read-only. My problems with it are mostly about using it as writable fs. Hence I think for this usecase it would actually be great.

> what kind of conflict is that? isn't that something one can fix?
> 
> i think overlayfs is actually fine, if used entirely read-only. My problems with it are mostly about using it as writable fs. Hence I think for this usecase it would actually be great.

If I recall correctly the issue is that due to the way the kernel's tracking of origin of files changes when overlayfs is involved, it is then not possible to enforce code integrity (ie: executables are from a signed verity volume), which is what the IPE LSM is about: https://microsoft.github.io/ipe/
SELinux further complicated things, although I cannot recall how. Sorry, not a kernel dev, and it was discussed long ago, so details are very fuzzy.

I'll spend some time and check if, with your proposal, I'd end up using overlay in my use case or the "leaf merge model" would apply, and if it's the latter then we are good.

@poettering I've pushed an initial stab at this - not yet full coverage of the multi-image feature, but most of the way there - would like to get some feedback first. Here's what I've done:

1) Added a primitive to compute the list of bind mounts and overlay mounts given two filesystem hierarchies, following the model you recommended
2) Enhanced MountImages: if the destination parameter is not specified, instead of erroring out it now instructs systemd to use the new primitive and do on overlay (this is quite nice and I have other uses for it!)
3) Enhanced portabled/portablectl to take --extra-image as a new parameter, which will end up using the above

It already supports parsing multiple extra images and attaching separate services, but IMHO it makes more sense to support that if we can join the namespaces as well (pod-like feature), so for now it's disabled.

The autodiscovery based on the naming convention is also not implemented, it's next on the list.

I thought about doing the discovery as part of the dissect-image logic rather than one layer above, but in the end I don't like that too much, because I really want to be able to override the default naming and pass custom paths.
Specifically, I need to reuse the same RootImage across many different services, and I need to be able to manage them individually - I don't see a clean way of doing that if the implementation was hidden in the dissect-image functions.

issue_context.title: RFE: add MountImages support in portable service for runtime, ephemeral composition of immutable OS and application images
issue_context.body:
**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**
The image model we use below portable services, as it is common, splits the OS/runtime and the application assets (eg: flatpak/snapd runtimes, docker layers), to centralize and speed up servicing of the OS/runtime.

Due to tight SLA, pipelines ownership rules and many many more really boring reasons, updating to fix CVEs in the base system libraries/binaries/components cannot be left to each application owner, and is instead owned by the platform. 
The assets are also immutable and signed (squashfs + dm-verity hash and signature), with different keys even, so at runtime a new asset cannot be built with a combination of the two (eg: appending the application squashfs to the runtime) as the private key material to sign is not accessible in any way. They cannot be extracted either, as the origin of each executed binary must be a dm-verity backed and signed volume (squashfs) for code integrity, and there's the IPE code integrity LSM enforcing this https://microsoft.github.io/ipe/
Which is a long-winded way to say that a runtime update cannot be bundled with each application and then re-deployed one by one as new monolithic images, but they have to be kept as separate, immutable objects, shipped separately by separate channels and composed at runtime.

So long story short, what we do right now is manually create the deploy directory for each portable service, mount /usr and /etc from the shared runtime squashfs, and then mount the application squashfs, and then finally point ```portablectl attach``` to that deploy directory to attach the composed runtime+application ""image"". We built a generator to create the units required per portable service to setup and teardown the whole thing.
It works, but it is clunky, slow, requires a lot of manual handling and downstream-only scripts and code to tie it together.

We'd really like to contribute a solution upstream to provide a nice, generalized, simple interface for this use case.

**Describe the solution you'd like**
A MountPaths service option is being added by https://github.com/systemd/systemd/pull/14451 which allows mounting arbitrary images at arbitrary paths in a service mount namespace.

All the process described above could use this new feature instead, and present users with a nice, usable and concise interface like

```portablectl attach --root /path/to/runtime/image /path/to/application/image```

portabled would then look into the application image for the portable service unit as usual, but then use the runtime image as RootDirectory/RootImage (and look into it for os-release), and use MountPaths to mount the portable service application image.

This could be done via a new DBUS method, like AttachImageWithRoot or something along those lines.

I'd like mount options to be appendable, like with MountPaths - so that the dm-verity support that was added in util-linux 2.35 can be used natively.

Does this sound like an acceptable feature to add?

Thanks!
comments:
@poettering here's my current thinking on this - now that MountImages has been merged as a primitive, duct-taping it in portabled is easy enough, and in fact I've got it working with a small diff that adds --root and --app-mount-point parameters to portablectl and a new dbus attach method. It works, all is well.

But - it seems to be it doesn't fit nicely with how images are handled for portabled and nspawn. It doesn't work with discovery and metadata extracting, as only the application image is linked in the portables/machines directory. It feels a bit shoe-horned in.

So what about the following instead. Establish a parent directory where all application images get mounted in, inside the guest namespace - eg: /run/systemd/app/<service name> (or any other path that fits). And then -

for single-filesystem images:

- extend /etc/portables and friends to support a drop-in hierarchy structure
- if foo.raw and foo.raw.d/bar.raw are present, foo.raw is RootImage and bar.raw is MountImages on /run/systemd/app/bar/
- same for directory-based images
- os-release is searched in foo.raw, units/nspawn commands are searched for in bar.raw

for GPT images:

- add a new partition GUID for app partitions, where the label is the name of the application and thus the mount point /run/systemd/app/<label>
- os-release is searched for in the root partition, units/nspawn commands are searched for in the app partition

What's nice about this scheme is that the next logical step could then be multiple application volumes/services/runners with a single root image, all sharing the same namespaces. Something like pods for podman/k8s.

Thoughts?

the error path is hosed here. you initialized the object to all zeroes via malloc0(), i.e. `m->fd` is going to be 0, which is a valid fd, and thus if this error path i hit we'l end up closing STDIN by accident. So you either have to initialize m->fd to -1 early on, or you drop the use of `_cleanup_` here for the object, and just insert a regular free() into this error path.
given that flags is zero anyway maybe call pass literal `UINT64_C(0)` here as argument?
it's now used for `runtime` as suggested
